data.title: The construction of Slavic hillforts – ramparts, gates and towers
data.excerpt: The oldest known fortifications continue the traditions of farming settlements that reach back to the Neolithic, and from the Bronze Age onwards strategically advantageous, naturally protected positions were sought out. The Slavs built the youngest hillforts of all – and in developmental terms the most accomplished. This article looks at how their defensive walls, ditches, gates and towers were actually built.
data.metaTitle: Construction of Slavic hillforts: ramparts, gates, towers
data.metaDescription: How the Slavs built their fortifications: grillage and box defensive walls, ditches, gates and the tower-like bastions of the Great Moravian period.

timeline.description: The culmination of the development of fortifications in the Great Moravian period – the hillfort’s function as a seat of power comes to the fore and the tower-like defensive bastion becomes the basic fortification element of double gates.

children.text: The oldest known fortifications continue the traditions of farming settlements whose developmental beginnings may be sought somewhere in the Neolithic, while from the Bronze Age onwards there is a clear trend of seeking out places with an advantageous strategic position and with natural protection afforded by the terrain. Nor are the
Slavs
any exception – the builders of the youngest hillforts, yet at the same time, in every respect and from a developmental point of view, of the
most accomplished hillforts

. Either upland hillforts or lowland fortified settlements in marshland were built, surrounded at first by a simple rampart with a palisade. Development, however, went on further, and in the 8th century we become witnesses to the refinement of hillforts, whether in military, settlement or social terms, with the culmination of this process occurring in the territory of present-day Slovakia in the Great Moravian period, generally in the 10th century. The Slavic hillfort thus enters the classic phase of its development; the function as a seat of power gradually comes to the fore, that is, the hillfort becomes the basis for the formation of future early feudal social relations, or rather entities. The ensuing turbulent social development is reflected in every direction, the constructional aspect not excepted. Let us therefore look at its specific forms, above all from the point of view of strategic military protection.

Progress occurs above all in the building of defensive walls. Out of the simple earthen rampart two basic types of defensive wall crystallise, namely the grillage type and the box type. The term „defensive wall“ is fully in order, because fortification structures begin to be ingeniously and technically elaborate.
The principle of
box construction

lies in building an outer and an inner face of the defensive wall formed of wooden planks, or of wickerwork within a framework of posts. The construction of the wall is stabilised by props (mostly on the inner side), or by an earthen rampart (mostly on the outer side). For greater strength and resistance the outer and inner walls are moreover linked transversely by anchoring beams, or by whole walls, again of wattle or entirely of timber, understandably of lesser massiveness in comparison with the outer and inner walls of the defensive wall. In this way a kind of chamber is created, from which this type of wall takes its name. The entire space of the chambers is filled with rammed earth right up to the upper edge of the inner wall. What arises is thus something like a wall-walk, protected by the outer wall, which is higher than the inner one and forms a palisade-like protection.
By
grillage construction

we mean the building of the core of the defensive wall by a system of individual horizons formed of beams laid tightly side by side. The beams are laid transversely to the course of the rampart – the so-called timber-and-earth grillage construction. A further possibility is the alternation of horizons with a transverse and a longitudinal placing of the beams – the so-called interleaved grillage construction. In the first case there are layers of earth between the individual timber horizons laid in the same direction; in the second case it is mostly a matter of tightly stacked layers of round timber alternating in direction. On the inner side the construction is usually strengthened by a wooden wall braced by props, as in the case of the box solution.

children.text: In the case of
interleaved construction

the outer wall, the front of the defensive wall, is formed as a simple sloping wall made of timber-and-earth material, similarly to the core of the defensive wall. If it is the first of the grillage construction types, that is, the alternation of earthen and timber layers, the front is in principle formed by a stone wall, with the beams of the individual grillages tied in directly, anchored in the stone wall. In the Polish area the interleaved construction was refined into the so-called hooked grillage construction, in which trunks with hook-like projecting branches were used for one of the layers; by these the beams of the next constructional level were caught from the outer side of the rampart.

In general, the constructional principles chosen were a question both of a sufficiency of material (good-quality timber, stone) and of regional tradition. While in the Polish area, for example, it was mainly the hooked grillage construction that was used, in the territory of present-day Slovakia the timber-and-earth grillage type predominated. Of course, combinations of various principles also occurred. For example a combination of timber-and-earth grillage construction with a box-built upper part of the defensive wall, or a box-built crown in combination with an interleaved grillage base.

In the literature we may sometimes also come across speculation about a specific form of rampart, the so-called vitrified rampart. This is supposedly a timber-and-earth, or timber-and-stone, construction in the manner of a grillage, which is additionally faced with a large quantity of timber. The rampart itself then comes into being by setting the timber facing alight, whereby, after the timber parts around and inside the rampart have burnt through, the high temperature causes partial melting and the subsequent fusing of its clay-and-stone material. There were arguments for and against, but in the end the view rejecting this theory prevailed. The position that took hold is that if we find the remains of such a „rampart“, it is probably a consequence of wartime fires, or the remains of smelting works. One of the main arguments against the existence of vitrified ramparts as one of the ways of realising a defensive wall, which seems cogent to me as well, is that it is hard to imagine the enormous effort that must have been expended on building the rampart itself and facing it with timber, only for it all to be „burnt“ in the end. For besides disproportionate labour, this method also presupposes a disproportionate consumption of material, especially timber, in relation to the result. We can therefore dismiss this type of defensive wall with a clear conscience.

Between the front of the defensive wall and the ditch lies the so-called berm. Like the front of the defensive wall, the berm too may be of stone or of clay. Together with the defensive wall itself it forms a single constructional unit and in some cases it even merges with its front.
The presence of a
defensive ditch
as part of the system of the defensive wall will probably surprise no one, since it is a classic element of fortifications and therefore, I think, needs no further comment.
Conversely, an important element in the construction of the Slavic defensive wall, especially from the defensive point of view, are the so-called záseky.
An abatis (zásek)

is a row of sharpened stakes set into the ground, angled towards the enemy. In constructional terms these obstacles are designed either as part of the berm, that is, they are placed behind the ditch, or they are set forward in the approach ground. They may be in a single row or in several rows.
Slavic defensive walls reached heights of even over 10 m, measured from the foot to the crown of the rampart. The height of the palisade itself, or the length of the abatis, was up to 2 m.
The most important place in the defensive wall is without doubt the
gate

. Since it is the most vulnerable point in the defensive system of a hillfort, special constructional solutions were needed to secure it. Around the year 800 the gates are still fairly simple, placed laterally or frontally. The essence of the lateral solution is to draw one of the arms of the rampart past the other, or to build a further rampart in front of the main defensive wall in the area of the approach to the gate. The strategic intention of this solution was that a would-be attacker had to advance towards the gate through the narrow passage thus created, while the defenders had the opportunity to attack his flank undisturbed. The second basic type is the simple frontal gate, provided with slightly projecting arms of the defensive wall, or conversely with the arms of the rampart drawn inwards. Again the point was the same, that is, the possibility of harrying the attackers in the area of the gate as effectively as possible. Tower-like defence of the entrance is not yet encountered in this period.
Conversely, in the classic phase of Slavic hillforts the
tower-like defensive bastion

becomes the basic fortification element. Gates are designed as double, with the defensive tower, as part of the defensive wall, placed between the two entrances. Massive double-entrance gates were a feature above all of central multi-level hillforts, distinguished by an advanced organisational structure. Double gates are often designed in a pincer-shaped manner, that is, the defensive walls curve into the interior of the hillfort, with the space behind the tower gradually narrowing. The defensive significance of this solution is, I think, obvious – that is, even if the gate doors are broken through, the attacker still stands a great chance of becoming the victim of a massacre. Of course, the classic single-entrance gates from the earlier period also remained in use, where the tower was placed directly above the entrance. Its defensive effectiveness was often multiplied by projecting it in front of the defensive wall itself, or by combining a non-projecting central tower with the setting back of one or both defensive walls in the area of the gate. Projecting towers are found in principle both in the case of frontal and in the case of lateral gates, where the bastion is pushed forward onto the arm defending the access corridor. In the last part of the classic phase we encounter a further multiplication of the number of towers; a pair of massive projecting towers on either side of the entrance gate is common. From the strategic defensive point of view, the analogy to the pincer solution in the case of double gates is the so-called tunnel solution in single-entrance gates.

children.text: The clear width of the gates was, understandably, chosen to be as narrow as possible for defensive reasons. In the case of double gates the width of each of the pair of entrances was around 2 m, rarely more. The dimension chosen was always a compromise between military and social-cum-commercial interests, where what mattered above all was that the gate should be passable by carts. Single-entrance gates tended to be wider, but at most 3.5 m. The minimum width of a gate has been determined from archaeological excavations as 1.6 m.

In connection with the towers it should be noted that, in order to secure the overall protection of a hillfort, separate watchtowers were often built as well, distributed in both the nearer and the more distant surroundings, securing important roads, fords and the like. These were mostly roofed structures, something in the manner of today’s hunting high seats, of course of greater height and dimensions.
The existence of a defensive ditch also presupposes the necessity of building
bridges

in the area of the gates. Of course, these structures were built as fixed ones; drawbridges are a matter only of the advanced medieval stone castles. In case of danger this problem was solved simply by pulling down the bridge or a part of it. Besides crossing defensive ditches, bridges also had their importance in the case of lowland fortified settlements, especially those on lakes or built on sea coasts, as was the case for example at Berhen-Lubchin or Wolin.

In conclusion, mention should still be made of the existence of roads within the areas of hillforts and often in their immediate surroundings as well. These were roads paved with stones or, more often, with timber – closely set planks mounted on longitudinal trunks sunk into the ground. There is reason to suppose that whole areas within the „built-up zone“ of hillforts could have been boarded over in a similar way, a kind of forerunner of today’s town squares.
